newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Apartheid killer says he needed no direct orders.
newsitem.headline: Apartheid killer says he needed no direct orders.

text.p: South Africa's secret police knew they were required to kill anti-apartheid activists even if their political masters gave no explicit orders, the country's truth commission heard on Tuesday.

"You would hear 'make a plan with so-and-so' or get a nod of the head or a wink-wink kind of attitude," former police hit squad leader Dirk Coetzee told the Truth and Reconciliation Commission in an application for amnesty.

Coetzee has admitted to killing two anti-apartheid activists, Griffiths Mxenge and Sizwe Kondile. He has been charged with the Mxenge murder but will not face trial if his amnesty application is approved.
No written instructions were ever given for the murder of anti-apartheid activists, Coetzee said.
"In the Mxenge case I was asked to 'make a plan' with him and this clearly meant to me that we had to kill him," said Coetzee, who served at the Vlakplaas secret police base outside Pretoria.
His successor as head of the base was Eugene de Kock, sentenced last month to two life terms and an additional 212 years in jail for a series of murders and lesser crimes.
One of the charges against de Kock was the attempted murder of Coetzee, who defected to the African National Congress in 1989 and began revealing secrets of the dirty war to bolster white rule.
Coetzee told the commission the security police had operated above the law "because the normal common law of the country was not sufficient to deal with the total revolutionary onslaught".
He said he had never questioned orders to kill activists from his superior officers for fear it would jeopardise his chances of promotion.
"I was only executing orders...stealing cars, murdering people, harassing people. Anything but legal police work," Coetzee said.
Coetzee is among several apartheid agents who have volunteered information to the commission, which is charged with compiling a full picture of human rights violations by all sides during white rule.

But the commission is locked in a row with President Nelson Mandela's ANC over whether individual members of the party need to seek amnesty for their actions during what they regard as a just war against oppression.
Commission chairman Desmond Tutu has threatened to quit the post, saying the ANC apparently felt it could declare itself blameless.
The ANC responded on Monday by saying Tutu had based his threat on an incorrect interpretation of the party's position.
